messages.subject: Bayesian Model Selection
parts:
Hi Stan,

Bob Carpenter asked me to post and ask this again in the group, so here is what happened so far:

I am using Stan for my Msc project and what I need to do is: sample different models, get the model evidences, and do Bayesian model selection. I am aware that this is not straightforward with Stan and that there is http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf

However, there is a function that is part of the tapas box http://www.translationalneuromodeling.org/tapas/ (it's called tapas_model_evidence_TI_trace) that can do this via ’thermodynamic integration’ (?). I would just need:
'two things , expected log likelihood from each chain and the corresponding chain temperature'

I gather I can get the former with something like:

generated quantities {
vector[N] log_lik;
for (n in 1:N){
log_lik[n] <- normal_log(y[n], X[n]*b, sigma);
}
}

Bob wrote:
"log_lik[n] is the likelihood for data item n and will be
calculated per draw.   The posterior mean of those draws is
the expected likelihood per item and their sum is the total expected
likelihood.

I don't know what you mean by "chain temperature" so I can't
suggest how to compute it.

I'm not the best person to talk to about WAIC --- you want
Andrew or Aki, and hence really want to write to our users list."


I am also not sure what chain temperature is, which is why I am writing
you, what I found online is: "Temp -- The temperature parameter for
heating the chains. The higher the temperature, the more likely the heated
chains are to move between isolated peaks in the posterior
distribution..." cf. http://mrbayes.sourceforge.net/Help/mcmc.html

Does anyone know about "chain temperatures"?

Many thanks!

David

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Model Selection
parts:
I would highly recommend that you don’t attempt these algorithms without
at least a basic understanding of what’s going on — they’re notoriously
difficult to implement with any reasonable quantification of error.

Firstly, the evidence/marginal likelihood is fundamentally different from
WAIC as they consider two completely different criteria for comparing
models.  See, for example, http://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02273.

On to thermodynamic algorithms.  The essential idea behind all of these
algorithms (see, for example, https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ss/1028905934)
is to interpolate between a simple base distribution (typically the prior) and a 
more complicated distribution (typically the posterior).  If we use the prior as 
our base distribution then we can write the interpolation as

pi(theta, beta) = (likelihood(theta) )^{beta} prior(theta),

where beta is an “inverse temperature”.  For beta = 0 we recover the prior
while beta = 1 yields the posterior.

Thermodynamic integration defines a partition of beta \in [0, 1] and then
computes the averages

L(beta) = E_{pi_{beta}} [ likelihood ] = \int dtheta pi(theta, beta) likelihood(theta)

If you wanted to use Stan to compute these intermediate averages then
you need to define a model for each pi(theta, beta), compute the likelihood
in generated quantities, and _then_ average the likelihood at each iteration
over the entire Markov chain.  You could throw these ( L(beta), beta) pairs
into some code such as the one you mentioned, but unless you choose
the partition of beta very carefully then you’re likely to get a biased answer.

Again, it’s technically feasible to compute these intermediate averages in
Stan but that that will require implementing pi(beta, theta) for each beta
and not just a single model, and doesn’t even get you halfway because
you still have to worry about how accurate the thermodynamic integration is.

messages.subject: Re: Bayesian Model Selection
parts:
Thanks for the advice!

I have now tried to model this so that Stan takes the likelihood^beta for sampling and accumulates the likelihood in the generated quantities:

model_code = {
'data {'
'    int<lower=0> N; // number of triad rounds times triads'
'    int<lower=0> K; // number of cooperation levels'
'    real<lower=0> beta; // chain temperature'
'    matrix[K,N] x; // predictor matrix'
'    matrix[K,N] xt; // predictor matrix trustees'
'    matrix[K,N] y; // outcome matrix'
'    matrix[2,16] p; // priors on parameters'
'}'
'parameters {'
'    matrix[K,K] A; // A matrix'
'    real<lower=0> sigma; // error scale'
'}'
'model {'
'    vector[K] xtemp;'
'    vector[K] xttemp;'
'    for (i in 1:4) {'
'        for (j in 1:4) {'
'            A[i,j] ~ normal(p[1,(i-1)*4+j], p[2,(i-1)*4+j]);'
'        }'
'    }'
'    for (n in 1:N) {'
'        xtemp <- col(x,n);'
'        xttemp <- col(xt,n);'
'        increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[1,n],A[1]*xtemp,sigma));'
'        increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[2,n],A[2]*xtemp,sigma));'
'        increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[3,n],A[3]*xttemp,sigma));'
'        increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[4,n],A[4]*xttemp,sigma));'
'    }'
'}'
'generated quantities {'
'    vector[K] xtemp;'
'    vector[K] xttemp;'
'    matrix[K,N] log_lik;'
'    for (n in 1:N) {'
'        xtemp <- col(x,n);'
'        xttemp <- col(xt,n);'
'        log_lik[1,n] <- normal_log(y[1,n],A[1]*xtemp,sigma);'
'        log_lik[2,n] <- normal_log(y[2,n],A[2]*xtemp,sigma);'
'        log_lik[3,n] <- normal_log(y[3,n],A[3]*xttemp,sigma);'
'        log_lik[4,n] <- normal_log(y[4,n],A[4]*xttemp,sigma);'
'    }'
'}'
};


This way the temperature does govern the behaviour of the sampler right? After sampling, I calculate the total log likelihood and pair them with the corresponding beta values (partitioned as (j/J)^5 for j=0,1,...,J and J=100). These pairs can then be used for the thermodynamic integration (e.g. with trapezoidal rule) to get the model evidence for BMS.

The only problem I have now is that for 16models*100chains(one per beta)*1000iterations this is taking days, any suggestions for computational efficiency?

Thanks a lot!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Model Selection
parts:
For efficiency, I'd first suggest a weakly informative prior on sigma.

Rewriting this:

> for (n in 1:N) {'
> ' xtemp <- col(x,n);'
> ' xttemp <- col(xt,n);'
> ' increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[1,n],A[1]*xtemp,sigma));'
> ' increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[2,n],A[2]*xtemp,sigma));'
> ' increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[3,n],A[3]*xttemp,sigma));'
> ' increment_log_prob(beta*normal_log(y[4,n],A[4]*xttemp,sigma));'

using vectorization as

increment_log_prob(beta * (normal_log(y[1], A[1] * x, sigma)
+ normal_log(y[2], A[2] * x, sigma)
+ normal_log(y[3], A[3] * xt, sigma)
+ normal_log(y[4], A[4] * xt, sigma)));

should be much more efficient.

I couldn't follow what was going on with this:

but I'm guessing it could also be vectorized by rearranging that
p matrix, though it looks like a different mean and sd for each A[i,j],
so there might not be much to gain there.

I'm afraid there's no way to speed up the generated quantities calc, but
that should be relatively fast as there are no gradient calcs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Model Selection
parts:
Thanks a lot! That did already make a considerable difference.

Since I only need the total expected likelihood per chain I could also speed up the generated quantities as:

'generated quantities {'
'    real log_lik;'
'    row_vector[K*N] xr;'
'    xr <- append_col(append_col(A[1]*x,A[2]*x),append_col(A[3]*xt,A[4]*xt));'
'    log_lik <- normal_log(yr,xr,sigma);'
'}'

where yr is the concatenated rows of y and already defined in the data section.

Anyway many thanks!
